summary: Defines managed objects related to the forwarding of IP packets in a way that works for both IPv4 and IPv6. It replaces RFC 2096 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This MIB gives an SNMP manager one table that shows the routes a node is forwarding on, in a form that works the same for IPv4 and IPv6. It replaces the older IPv4-only table and also replaces the two separate counters that said how many routes had been thrown away.

questions: what is the ip forwarding table mib
how does snmp read a routing table
subtitle: The standard SNMP table for reading, and optionally editing, a router's IPv4 and IPv6 forwarding table.

tldr.problem: Managers could read an IPv4 routing table through SNMP, but the objects were tied to IPv4, and the counters for discarded routes existed in two separate, version-specific forms.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a single inetCidrRouteTable whose index and columns use the version-independent InetAddress types, so the same table describes IPv4 and IPv6 routes. Two global objects, inetCidrRouteNumber and inetCidrRouteDiscards, sit alongside it.
tldr.outcome: One table now covers both IP versions, and the discarded-route count is a single object. A read-only conformance statement was added for implementations that only want to read. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2096.

today: RFC 4292 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2096, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Forwarding Table for Both IP Versions
sections.content:
The RFC defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing objects related to the forwarding of Internet Protocol packets, in an IP version-independent manner. It notes at the outset that the MIB definition does not support multiple instances based on the same address family type, but that it does support an instance of the MIB per address family.

The memo sits inside the Internet-Standard Management Framework, and points readers to Section 7 of RFC 3410 for a detailed overview. Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB, and are generally accessed through SNMP. The memo specifies a MIB module compliant to SMIv2, described in STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The module is named IP-FORWARD-MIB and is placed at ip 24. Its own revision history records three versions: the initial version published as RFC 1354, revised to support CIDR routes and published as RFC 2096, and the IPv4 and IPv6 version-independent revision published as RFC 4292, which made minimal changes to the original RFC 2096 MIB to allow easy upgrade of existing IPv4 implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB gives an SNMP manager one table that shows the routes a node is forwarding on, in a form that works the same for IPv4 and IPv6. It replaces the older IPv4-only table and also replaces the two separate counters that said how many routes had been thrown away.

sections.title: One Table and Two Counters
sections.content:
The MIB consists of one current table and two current global objects.

inetCidrRouteNumber indicates the number of current routes. The RFC gives the reason for having it: primarily to avoid having to read the table in order to determine this number. It is a Gauge32 and gives the number of current inetCidrRouteTable entries that are not invalid.

inetCidrRouteDiscards counts the number of valid routes that were discarded from inetCidrRouteTable for any reason. It is a Counter32, and this object replaces the ipRoutingDiscards and ipv6DiscardedRoutes objects. Discarded route entries do not appear in the table, and one possible reason for discarding an entry would be to free up buffer space for other route table entries.

The inetCidrRouteTable provides the ability to display IP version-independent multipath CIDR routes. It is described as this entity's IP routing table, with a reference to Section 6.6 of RFC 1213, The IP Group.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has one table and two counters. The first counter says how many routes are in the table, so a manager does not have to read the whole table to find out. The second says how many valid routes were discarded, which is a new object that replaces the IPv4 and IPv6 versions of that counter.

sections.title: What It Replaces
sections.content:
Section 4.1 describes the relationship between the objects in this MIB and the tables and objects in other MIB modules, several of which are deprecated or obsolete.

The ipRouteTable object was originally defined in RFC 1213, and was updated by ipForwardTable in RFC 1354. The ipForwardTable replaced the ipRouteTable, and was in turn obsoleted by the ipCidrRouteTable defined in RFC 2096. RFC 1354 also introduced ipForwardNumber, which reflects the number of entries in ipForwardTable and was obsoleted by ipCidrRouteNumber.

In RFC 2096 the ipCidrRouteTable and ipCidrRouteNumber were introduced. The ipCidrRouteTable supports multipath IP routes having the same network number but differing network masks, and the number of entries in that table is reflected in ipCidrRouteNumber. Both are deprecated by the definitions in this MIB.

RFC 2011 contains the ipRoutingDiscards object, which counts the number of valid routes removed from the ipCidrRouteTable, and the corresponding ipv6DiscardedRoutes object is defined in RFC 2465. Both are deprecated in favour of the version-independent inetCidrRouteDiscards.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC traces the history. The route table first appeared in MIB-II, was replaced by the forward table, and was then replaced by the CIDR route table in RFC 2096, which is what this document deprecates. The two discard counters came from RFC 2011 and RFC 2465, one for each IP version, and are replaced here by a single version-independent object.

sections.title: The inetCidrRouteTable
sections.content:
Each row of the table is a particular route to a particular destination under a particular policy, as reflected in the inetCidrRoutePolicy object. Dynamically created rows survive an agent reboot. The RFC warns implementers that if the total number of elements, octets or sub-identifiers, in inetCidrRouteDest, inetCidrRoutePolicy and inetCidrRouteNextHop exceeds 111, then the OIDs of column instances in this table have more than 128 sub-identifiers and cannot be accessed using SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3.

The row is indexed by six objects: inetCidrRouteDestType, inetCidrRouteDest, inetCidrRoutePfxLen, inetCidrRoutePolicy, inetCidrRouteNextHopType and inetCidrRouteNextHop. The address type objects are of the InetAddressType type, and only address types that may appear in an actual routing table are allowed as values. The destination address and the prefix length must be consistent: when the value of inetCidrRouteDest, excluding the zone index if one is present, is x, then the bitwise logical-AND of x with the mask formed from inetCidrRoutePfxLen MUST be equal to x. If not, the index pair is not consistent and an inconsistentName error must be returned on SET or CREATE requests. The policy object is opaque, without any defined semantics, and exists to serve as an additional index that may delineate between multiple entries.

The remaining columns carry the operational information. inetCidrRouteIfIndex is the ifIndex of the local interface through which the next hop should be reached, and a value of 0 is valid and means no interface is specified. inetCidrRouteType says what the route does: other(1), not specified by this MIB; reject(2), a route that discards traffic and returns an ICMP notification, used in some protocols as a means of correctly aggregating routes; local(3), a local interface; remote(4), a remote destination; and blackhole(5), a route that discards traffic silently. The RFC notes that local(3) refers to a route whose next hop is the final destination, while remote(4) refers to one whose next hop is not. Routes that do not result in traffic forwarding or rejection should not be displayed, even if the implementation keeps them stored internally.

inetCidrRouteProto is the routing mechanism by which the route was learned, and the RFC notes that including gateway routing protocol values is not intended to imply that hosts should support those protocols. inetCidrRouteAge is the number of seconds since the route was last updated or otherwise determined to be correct, with the caution that no semantics of too old can be implied except through knowledge of the routing protocol. inetCidrRouteNextHopAS is the Autonomous System Number of the next hop, whose semantics depend on the routing protocol, and which should be zero when unknown or not relevant.

There are five metric columns, inetCidrRouteMetric1 to inetCidrRouteMetric5, each an Integer32 whose meaning is set by the routing protocol and which should be -1 when the metric is not used. inetCidrRouteStatus is a RowStatus used according to row installation and removal conventions, and a row cannot be modified while its status is active(1).
sections.plainLanguage: Each row is one route, identified by six things: the type and address of the destination, the length of the network mask, a policy identifier, and the type and address of the next hop. The other columns say which interface to use, whether the route is local, remote, rejected or a black hole, which routing protocol learned it, how old it is, the autonomous system of the next hop, five metric values, and a row status used to add and remove rows.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects in this MIB module have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The RFC states that support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The inetCidrRouteTable contains routing and forwarding information that is critical to the operation of the network node, especially a router, and allowing unauthenticated write access to this table can compromise the validity of the forwarding information.

Some of the readable objects may also be considered sensitive, and the RFC says it is thus important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to them, and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network. The inetCidrRouteTable contains routing information that can be used to compromise a network: specifically, it can be used to construct a map of the network in preparation for a denial-of-service attack on the network infrastructure. The inetCidrRouteProto object identifies the routing protocols in use within a network, and that information can be used to determine how such an attack should be launched.

The RFC notes that SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and that even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is still no control over who on the secure network may read or change the objects in this MIB. It recommends that implementers consider the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of earlier versions is not recommended. It then notes that it is a customer or operator responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB module is properly configured to give access only to those principals that have legitimate rights.
sections.plainLanguage: The table holds the routing information a router depends on, so giving anyone write access to it can break forwarding. Even reading it is sensitive, because the addresses in it can be used to draw a map of the network. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its authentication and privacy features, and says earlier versions should not be deployed.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2096
sections.content:
Section 7 of the RFC lists the ways in which this document obsoletes RFC 2096.

  1. It replaces ipCidrRouteTable with inetCidrRouteTable, which applies to the corresponding objects and conformance statements.
  2. It uses the InetAddress textual convention to support IP version-independent implementations of the forwarding MIB, giving common forwarding MIB support for IPv4 and IPv6.
  3. It creates a read-only conformance statement to support implementations that only wish to retrieve data.
  4. It creates the inetCidrRouteDiscards object to replace the deprecated ipRoutingDiscards and ipv6DiscardedRoutes objects.

The RFC notes that the inetCidrRouteTable retains the logical structure of the ipCidrRouteTable, in order to allow the easy upgrade of existing IPv4 implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things changed. The IPv4-only route table was replaced with a version-independent one, the InetAddress type is used so that IPv4 and IPv6 share the same definitions, a read-only conformance statement was added for managers that only want to look, and a single discard counter replaced the two version-specific ones.

viz.caption: THE SIX OBJECTS THAT IDENTIFY A ROUTE ROW

items.title: DestType
items.text: The type of the destination address.

items.title: Dest
items.text: The destination address of the route.

items.title: PfxLen
items.text: The number of leading one bits in the network mask.

items.title: Policy
items.text: An opaque identifier that may separate several entries.

items.title: NextHopType
items.text: The type of the next hop address.

items.title: NextHop
items.text: The address of the next hop.
